sections.heading: One-Pot Soft-Template Synthesis of Nanostructured Copper-Supported Mesoporous Carbon FDU-15 Electrocatalysts for Efficient CO2 Reduction
sections.text: Nihat Ege Şahin,[a] Clément Comminges,*[a] Anthony Le Valant,[a] Julien Kiener,[b] Julien Parmentier,[b] Teko W. Napporn,[a] Georgian Melinte,[c] Ovidiu Ersen,[c] and Kouakou B. Kokoh*[a] Copper-supported mesoporous carbon nanocatalysts (Cu/FDU15) were synthesized using an easy and convenient one-pot soft-template method for low-overvoltage CO2 electroreduction. TEM imaging revealed the presence of large Cu nanoparticles (diameter 140 nm) with Cu2O nanoparticles (16 nm) as an additional phase. From the electron tomography observations, we found that the copper particles were placed inside and on the exterior surface of the porous FDU-15 support, providing an accessible surface for electrocatalytic reactions. CO2 electrolyses showed that the mesostructured Cu/FDU-15-350 cathode materials were active towards CO2 conversion to formic acid with 22 % Faradaic efficiency at a remarkably low overpotential of 290 mV, hydrogen being the only side-product. The catalyst’s activity correlates to the calculated metallic surface area, as determined from a geometrical model, confirming that the mesoporous channels act as a diffusion path for the CO2 molecule, and that the whole Cu surface is accessible to CO2, even if particles are entrapped in the carbon matrix.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Energy generation using non-renewable fossil fuels is associated with greenhouse gases emissions, mainly carbon dioxide (CO2), which is the main cause of the global warming. Several studies have been strategically developed in order to valorise the CO2 molecule, particularly, the processes that take advantage of the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) in order to produce a variety of useful products including fuels or other derived hydrocarbons.[1] Among the various efficient CO2 conversion approaches, the electrochemical CO2RR route promises a sustainable process for generating liquid fuels such as formic acid (HCOOH),[2] which is an attractive fuel as well as an energetic vector. Especially, it has been used as a fuel in direct formic acid fuel cells (DFAFCs)[3] and as a sustainable chemical for hydrogen storage.[4] The recent developments in DFAFCs revealed that formic acid is one of -promising energy sources for powering portable electronic devices and fuel cell vehicles. The drawbacks on storage capacity and transportation[5] of molecular hydrogen under high pressure are handled by the virtue of production of formic acid as a reversible source of hydrogen storage. Practically, it is more convenient and economic to use hydrogen-containing materials,[6] namely formic acid, which can be broken down under ambient conditions, instead of using highly-pressurized H2 gas. Hence, it is estimated that global demand of safer and low cost hydrogen storage materials will dramatically increase for energyrelated applications. Thus, there is an increased interest in developing the technological CO2-converting devices that improve the Faradaic selectivity in the field of CO2 electroreduction to formic acid. To sum up, one of the objectives of this study is to propose an electrochemical approach for the CO2-to-HCOOH production that can help to eliminate some obstacles such as hydrogen storage and transportation, and mitigates the dependence of non-renewable fossil fuels. Significant efforts have been made for understanding the electrochemical CO2 conversion both in homogeneous [7] and heterogeneous catalysis[8] approaches, exposing different reaction pathways.[9] Carbon dioxide, as the last oxidation state of carbonaceous organics, is extremely stable and its electrochemical conversion requires a high overpotential due to its initial reduction to highly energetic bent CO2 * radical anion from a single electron transfer. Evidences of the latter adsorbed species were previously revealed by in-situ FTIR spectroscopy[10] and Raman spectroscopy[11] at Pb, Pt and Ag electrode surfaces. Over the past few decades, challenging electrode materials such as metals,[1c,12] metal oxides,[13] and metal-organic com-

It is also critical to highlight that many efforts were devoted in the development of lab-scale and scale-up prototype electrolyzers, including H-type electrochemical cell,[15] filter-press cell,[16] high-temperature solid-oxide electrolyzer[17] that operate with active, stable and conducting electrocatalysts.[18] Different carbon substrates have been preferably used as supporting materials due to their unique advantages given by their physical and chemical properties, including electrical and thermal conductivity as well as high mechanical strength. In catalytic applications, collective properties of metal-supported catalysts can be tuned by controlling the three-dimensional distribution of metallic nanoparticles.[19] Nowadays, the use of mesoporous carbon materials as catalyst supports or even as metal-free catalysts is increasing due to their outstanding surface chemistry and tunable porosity properties. Particularly, the large surface area and high porosity of these materials promote the homogeneous dispersion of the metal nanoparticles over the support. The accessible internal surface of the pores network associated with the microporous nature of the carbon walls yield materials with large surface area and large adsorption capacity of gases via physisorption interactions.[20] Porous carbon materials, with controlled mesoporosity can be achieved with ordered mesoporous carbon materials prepared either by the hard-templating[21] or more recently soft-templating process.[22] The later is based on the use of a soluble carbon precursor, either synthetic (e. g. phenolic resin) or biosourced[23] and a porogen agent (usually an amphilic block copolymer). Their self-assembly in solution or during their evaporation (named Evaporation Induced Self-Assembly process (EISA) leads to an ordered composite mesophase (resin/template) which is further converted by heat-treatment in inert atmosphere (carbonization) to an ordered mesoporous carbon. Amongst the ordered mesoporous carbon materials, FDU-15 has an hexagonal pore structure with high surface area, high pore volume and tunable pore diameters. It is a promising candidate as a catalyst support due to its good thermal stability and chemical inertness towards unwanted reactions. This softtemplate process can integrate soluble metallic precursor to yield nanocomposites MXn/C (M = metal, X = C, N, O, S…) with metal-based nanoparticles trapped in the mesoporous carbon matrix. It has been shown that this process is highly versatile, easy to perform and direct (one step with the one-pot procedure).[24] The main limitation is related to the minimum temperature of calcination required to pyrolyse the porogen agent and free the porosity (usually for polyoxamer of Pluronic type used around 350 8C). Among the different metals that can be used to activate and electrochemically convert the CO2 molecule, several studies have already been reported on Cu and Cu2O electrodes and provided sound evidence on their improved performances towards the CO2 electroreduction reaction. [25] Based on the recent findings in the field of catalyst synthesis, we prepared an alternative electrocatalyst for CO2 catalysis based on electroactive copper particles embedded in a mesoporous carbon matrix. This electrocatalyst is prepared in a single step using the one-pot soft templating route where Cu
particles are generated in-situ during the carbonisation of the mesophase. In-depth characterizations of the material, using complementary techniques (3D- TEM, N2 physisorption and particle morphology models based on X-Ray diffraction) are employed to demonstrate that this synthesis allow a particular structuration of the catalyst which ensure a good dispersion of Cu particles in the carbon matrix and their complete accessibility to CO2 molecules through the porous network. This material has also revealed a high selectivity for CO2 electroreduction to formic acid at remarkably low overpotential. Finally, a structural model based on the truncated octahedron shape for Cu clusters is developed to evaluate the accessible metallic surface area and is used to demonstrate that confined Cu clusters embedded in the carbon matrix are still accessible for the CO2 molecule. This particular growth of the Cu particles allows increasing the catalytic current for the CO2RR.

sections.heading: 2. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
Figure 1 depicts N2 adsorption-desorption isotherms (a) and the corresponding BJH pore size distribution curves (b) for Cu/FDU15-350 and Cu/FDU-15-500 catalysts. Both materials demonstrate the characteristic type-IV shape isotherms with a similar hysteresis loop (type-H1), revealing the occurrence of pore condensation with the characteristics of a cylindrical pore

As shown in Figure 1a, typical presence of micropores was also observed in the low relative pressure range. It appears that Cu/FDU-15-350 catalyst has higher nitrogen up-take at low and high pressures than Cu/FDU-15-500, leading to higher surface area and total pore volume (430 m2 g 1 and 0.47 cm3 g 1 compared to 347 m2 g 1 and 0.33 cm3 g 1 respectively). The mesopore size distributions (Figure 1b) are relatively narrow with pore diameters centered around 7.4 and 6.5 nm for the Cu/FDU-15-350 and Cu/FDU-15-500, respectively. The surface area, pore volume and pore size are all decreased by the carbonization temperature and are summarized in Table S1. A comparison of differential thermal and thermo-gravimetric (DT/ TG) analysis curves of prepared materials are given in Figure S1. TG curves state the real metal loading of the catalysts whereas DT curves highlight the differences on the oxidation temperature of metallic copper and mesoporous carbon FDU-15 support. The loss of weight (i) below 100 8C corresponds to water desorption in the catalytic powder. Thereafter, a second weight loss composed is observed between 180 and 400 8C. It could be assigned to oxidation/decomposition of the C-rich polymer arising from the phenolic resin and for Cu/FDU-15350 8C uncomplete decomposition of the template. Concomitantly, three exothermal contributions were observed which correspond to the oxidation of the polymers, metallic copper and Cu2O. The real metal loadings for the Cu/FDU-15-350 and Cu/FDU-15-500 catalysts are found to be 13.6 and 17.6 wt.%, respectively after subtraction of adsorbed water content (ca 5 wt.%) and taking into account CuO formation during TGA in air (as evidenced by post XRD analysis and not reported herein). X-ray diffraction patterns of the Cu/FDU-15-350 and Cu/ FDU-15-500 are illustrated in Figure 2. All the phases were identified by referring to the Joint Committee on Powder Diffraction Standards International Centre for Diffraction Data
(JCPDS-ICDD) database. The diffraction lines at 43.298, 50.438, 74.138, 89.938 and 95.148 correspond, respectively to the planes (111), (200), (220), (311) and (222) of face-centered cubic (fcc) copper with a lattice constant of a = b = c = 3.6150 Å (reference code 00-004-0836). Diffraction patterns display sharp and narrow peaks, confirming the high degree of crystallinity, with traces of NaCl resulting from the successive addition of NaOH and HCl during the synthesis (Figure S2). Calculations made from Scherrer equation on the Cu (111) plane give average crystallite sizes of 42.2 and 46.9 nm for the Cu/FDU-15-350 and Cu/FDU-15-500 materials, respectively. Lattice parameter of 3.6156 Å for Cu/FDU-15-350 and 3.6162 Å for Cu/FDU-15-500 materials are in good agreement with the theoretical value of 3.6150 Å for Cu. The Williamson-Hall procedure allows additional information on the microstructure via the size-induced and strain-induced broadenings as a function of 2q. It is shown in Figure S3 that the integral peak width (db =bhklcos(q)/l) slightly depends on the values of b = 2sin(q)/l, suggesting that XRD patterns are affected by micro-strain as well. The microstrain factors were estimated at about 0.15 and 0.10 % for Cu/ FDU-15-350 and Cu/FDU-15-500 catalysts, respectively, indicating growth of the Cu particles in the porous structure without deformation.
Cu/FDU-15 samples were examined by TEM. The hexagonal array of mesopores (transversal view) or the fringes (longitudinal view), typical of FDU-15 phase, were observed as shown in
Figure 3. It indicates that the mesostructure of the carbon is stable despite the presence of copper salt during the softtemplating process and its reduction to copper particles within the mesostructure.
Figure 4 depicts the cross section transmission electron microscopy (CS-TEM) observations of Cu/FDU-15 samples with different calcination temperatures and the corresponding mean particle size (Dm.p) distribution histograms based on the observation of more than 200 particles. As can be seen at this magnification, the mesoporous carbon FDU-15 support is composed of large Cu nanoparticles well dispersed inside the mesoporous carbon support. The dispersed copper nanoparticles throughout the mesostructure can be seen as black spots in the CS-TEM micrographs (Figures 4a and 4b). A particle growth is observed as the mean particle size of the as-prepared Cu/FDU-15 catalysts apparently increases from 141 nm to 196 nm when the calcination temperature is raised from 350 to 500 8C. It should be emphasized that the obtained catalysts are composed of bulky metallic Cu as confirmed by EDX analysis (see Figure S4a and b, SI). Beside large Cu nanoparticles, small

Cu2O particles (16 nm) were also evidenced for Cu/FDU-15-350 (Figure S4a and c). Careful analysis on copper particles was performed using bright and dark field measurements for Cu/FDU-15 samples (Figure S5 and Figure S6). Copper appears as big particles in bright field for Cu/FDU-15-350 (Figures S5a, c) and for Cu/FDU15-500 (Figures. S6a, c). Cu2O structure appears in dark ones (Figure S5(b) and Figure S6(b)) as a shell surrounding Cu particles (Figure S6) or as hollow particles (Figure S5 d). Fast Fourier transform (FFT) analyses were also performed on darkfield mode images (Figure S5(e) and Figure S6(e)) and confirmed the crystal structure of Cu2O (111) along a [011] zone axis. The as-deduced parameters are listed in Table S2. Therefore, particles appear as core type-copper particles (Figure S6c) with a shell type-Cu2O structure with a thickness of ca. 8 nm (Figure S6d). Regarding hollow Cu2O nanoparticles, it is wellknown that the growth of Cu2O layer on copper nanoparticles causes formation of voids at the interface between core copper and the outer Cu2O shells. [26] As the contrast of high angle annular dark field STEM (HAADF-STEM) images is strongly dependent on the atomic number, this technique is very useful in studying composite materials due to its ability to distinguish between their different phases. The HAADF-STEM images shown in Figure 5a and 5c together with their corresponding bright-field STEM images (Figure 5b and 5d) reveal the Cu nanoparticles distribution in the FDU-15 support. One can observe the different sharpness of Cu nanoparticles with some of them appearing in perfect focus while other out-of-focus. This observation can be correlated with the limited depth of focus of a Cs-corrected STEM probe and shows that the nanoparticles are distributed on multiple levels in the FDU-15 support. The inserted images from Figure 5a and 5b show that some nanoparticles are crossed by holes formed during the oxidization process
through the Kirkendall oxidation mechanism. The voids create defects in the crystalline structure and further increase the metallic surface area. An explanation for the formation of voids when nanoparticles are in contact with the FDU-15 substrate is governed by the different diffusion rates of the involved chemical species along the crystallographic defects within the particles. The Cu particles population can be split into spherical and rod like shapes, with a majority of sphere like particles. The 3D distribution of the Cu nanoparticles was revealed using electron tomography. Bright-field STEM signal was used for creating the 3D reconstructions due to its sensitivity to lowatomic number materials, i. e. mesoporous carbon. Figure 6 show a selection of longitudinal slices (perpendicular to the electron beam) through the reconstructed volume of the Cu/ FDU-15-350 (a–d) and Cu/FDU-15-500 (e–h) composites. The analysis of the reconstructed volumes reveals that the nanoparticles are distributed both on the surface and inside the FDU-15 support (see also supporting video). As expected, nanoparticles found on the external surface of the grains are more affected by the Kirkendall effect during the oxidation. It appears also that Cu particles are surrounded by a void in the mesoporous matrix (white zones around particles observed in Figure 6). This phenomenon has already been observed in Pd/C system prepared by the same one-pot soft-template process.[24b] This additional porosity is supposed to promote accessibility of the whole Cu particles to the reacting species. Figure 7 presents the 3D models of the composites (a, c) and Cu nanoparticles alone (b, d). The voids and the faceted morphology of the nanoparticles can be clearly observed.

sections.heading: 2.1. CO2 Electroreduction on Cu/FDU-15 Materials
sections.text:
Prior to carrying out long-term electrolysis on CO2 by setting a suitable electrode potential (chronoamperometric experiments), voltammetric characterizations of the Cu/FDU-15 as well as
FDU-15 materials were performed in 0.5 mol L 1 NaHCO3. The cyclic voltammograms (CVs) of the two mesoporous carbon samples synthesized without Cu precursor show that there is obviously no electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 in the absence of Cu (Figure S7). Figure 8 displays the CVs of Cu/FDU-15-350 and
Cu/FDU-15-500 electrodes under inert gas (N2) at pH = 8.54 or CO2-saturated (pH = 7.14) aqueous electrolyte. The electrochemical behavior of these catalysts prepared with the same electrode loading (precisely 103 mg of metal cm 2) were examined in a conventional three-electrode cell configuration. There is plenty of evidence in the literature regarding the role of the Cu/Cu2O/CuO redox species at copper electrodes in different buffer solutions[27] or in alkaline media.[28] As shown in Figure 8, the CVs exhibit two similar characteristic peaks related to the formation of Cu2O (a1/c1) and CuO (a2/c2). The first peak (a1) indicates the formation of oxidized copper Cu2O and the second one (a2) represents the transformation of Cu2O into CuO via electrochemical reactions as expressed in following Equations 1, 2. In the negative potential going-scan, the cathodic peak (c2) at 0.45 V represents the reduction of CuO to Cu2O. Another cathodic peak (c1) at 0.24 V can be attributed to the reduction of Cu2O to Cu 0 (Figure 8).

A broad CO2-reduction peak (c3), located at ca. 0.41 V is evidently observed in the presence of CO2. As pointed out above, the CO2-reduction current density increases with Cu/ FDU-15-350 (Figure 8a) (ip,350 c3 = 7.51 mA cm 2) compared to the Cu/FDU-15-500 sample (Figure 8b) (ip,500 c3 = 5.53 mA cm 2). The ratio ip,350 c3 / ip,500 c3 of 1.35 can be explained by a smaller nanoparticle size (as determined by TEM, Figure 4) and higher surface area of the carbon matrix. copper originating from hydrated CuO. It should be noted that this characteristic anodic peak most likely corresponds to the Cu2O3 that appears in the course of oxidation of copper [29] as well. In previously reported study,[30] three oxidation states of copper corresponding to Cu0/Cu+, Cu+/Cu2 + and Cu2 +/Cu3 + were well distinguished in alkaline media. Those CVs (Figure S9) are qualitatively similar to the one obtained on a Cu catalyst deposited onto a non mesoporous carbon (synthesis of Cu/ Vulcan S8). The c3 catalytic peak current in this case is 6.13 mA cm 2. This value is between Cu/FDU-15-350 (7.51 mA cm 2) and Cu/FDU-15-500 (5.53 mA cm 2).This tends to show that the textural properties of carbon do not mainly affect the electrocatalytic reaction. The observed differences in catalytic current are therefore a consequence of the Cu particles size and morphology. One of the main drawbacks associated with the CO2 electroreduction process concerns, in terms of energy required for its activation, the overpotential according to the nature of the electrode surface. To overcome this issue and to determine the suitable electrode potential value for optimizing the CO2 reduction, long-term electrolysis experiments were carried out at six different potentials from 0.47 to 0.82 V vs. RHE with a constant catalyst loading on the electrode (3.18 mg cm 2) in CO2-saturated 0.5 mol L 1 NaHCO3 electrolytes (Figure 9a and Figure 9b). Whatever the cathode material, two reaction products (HCOOH and CO) resulting from the CO2 reduction are obtained; hydrogen production is a parallel Faradaic reaction which increases with overpotential (Figure 9a and Figure 9b).
The Faradaic efficiency for formic acid reaches an optimum value of 17 % (Figure 9a) and 8 % (Figure 9b) at the potential of
0.72 V when the catalyst loading is 3.18 mg cm 2 for the Cu/ FDU-15-350 and Cu/FDU-15-500, respectively. At more cathodic potentials the CO production tends towards zero and the Faradaic efficiency for the HER remains at ca. 80 %. The high selectivity obtained for formic acid compared to CO can be explained by carbon at the Cu subsurface, as it was demonstrated from DFT calculations.[31] It is known that methane (CH4) and ethylene (C2H4) are produced on copper based electrodes[12,32] by means of different reaction mechanisms.[9a,32] Recently, Roberts et al.[33] distinguished the role of the onset potential on the formation of hydrocarbon products. They highlighted that formation of CH4 is observed at potentials between 0.90 and 0.99 V vs. RHE, explaining why hydrocarbons were not detected in our study.
Figure 9c and Figure 9d provide evidences that the catalyst loading on the electrode can be a key parameter in the improvement of the CO2 reduction reaction process. This can be explained by the mesostructure of the FDU-15 substrate composed of mesopores capable of playing an important role in the mass transport phenomenon. Setting constant the electrode potential at 0.72 V when the previous chronoamperometric measurements were optimized, the variation of the catalyst loading deposited onto the electrode permits the enhancement of the concentration of the molecule of interest, herein HCOOH. Indeed, the Faradaic efficiency for formic acid reaches, with 4.77 mg cm 2, a maximum of 21.3 % and 17.5 %, at the surface of Cu/FDU-15-350 (Figure 9c) and Cu/FDU-15-500 (Figure 9d), respectively. At this mass loading, the Faradaic efficiency towards CO remains very low and increases at 6.36 mg cm 2, suggesting that a less accessibility of the reactant in the mesopores is rather favorable to a CO2-to-CO conversion. The HER process issued from the reduction of the solvent is high in all the cases (80 %), which concerns a part of current non-utilized for the main CO2 reduction.
As the cyclic voltammograms of the two catalysts (Figure 8) are only differing in terms of observed current densities and as the product distribution is similar, the differences are likely to be due to a difference in the exposed metallic specific surface area. The latter can be estimated by using the model described in the following section.

sections.heading: 2.2. Model Calculation: Determination of the Metallic Specific Surface Area of Copper with the Crystallite Size Determined by XRD (dXRD)

It is of 12.4 and 8.9 m2 gCu 1 for Cu/FDU-15-350 and Cu/FDU-15-500, respectively (Table S1) and 10.3 m2 gCu 1 for the Cu/Vulcan reference material (Table S3). For the mesoporous materials, the surface ratio of 1.39 matches the ratio of c3 peak current densities of 1.35. The higher metallic specific surface area leads to higher current densities during electrolyses as well, and yields a slightly higher faradaic yield for HCOOH production. This correlation of electrocatalytic activity to the exposed metallic surface area (Figure S10) evidences that the Cu nanoparticles, which are mostly located inside the mesoporous carbon matrix, are still accessible to the substrate. The mesoporous channels are therefore acting as diffusion path for CO2 that is still able to react on the embedded Cu surface.

sections.heading: 3. Conclusions
sections.text:
The development of low-cost and effective catalysts with selective surface is crucial for lowering overpotential and for an efficient CO2 electroreduction process. Mesoporous carbon FDU-15 supported copper (Cu/FDU-15) catalysts were synthesized by the one-pot soft template method. According to the material heat-treatment at 350 or 500 8C, slightly different textural properties such as surface area, pore volume and pore diameter were obtained for Cu/FDU-15 catalysts. It can be suggested that the higher calcination temperature leads to an increase in the copper crystallite size and to a decrease in the lattice-strain. The surface morphology and composition of the as-prepared materials were examined using several advanced techniques. From the 3D-TEM observations, it was found that copper particles exist both inside and on the external surface of the FDU-15 carbon support. Cross-section TEM and EDX measurements revealed the difference of the Cu/Cu2O structure on the catalysts morphology. The Cyclic voltammetry (CV) analysis confirmed that the Cu/FDU-15-350 catalyst exhibited higher reduction current density under CO2-saturated measurements. If H2 production issued from the solvent reduction is considered as a parallel reaction, the CO2 conversion leads mainly to formic acid. The Faradaic efficiency towards this molecule was 21.3 % at 0.72 V vs. RHE. Under these conditions, the second carbonaceous reaction production (CO) has a low formation rate when the cathode loading increases up to 4.77 mg cm 2. In order to account for the current densities differences, a model for determining the accessible metallic copper surface area was developed. The catalyst’s activity correlates to the exposed metallic surface area, what gives evidence that the embedded Cu nanoparticles are still accessible to the substrate. This particular result shows that the one-pot soft-templating method is an excellent strategy for the development of three-dimensional electrodes, thus paving the way to the efficient design of electrocatalysts.

sections.heading: Synthesis of Mesostructured Cu/FDU-15 Catalyst
sections.text: For the synthesis of copper supported mesoporous carbon catalyst, phenolic resin was the carbon source, amphiphilic triblock copolymer Pluronic F-127 (Sigma-Aldrich) the soft-template of mesoporosity and copper(II)nitrate trihydrate (Cu(NO3)2.3H2O (Merck, 99.5 %)) the metallic copper precursor. The synthesis of the phenolic resin precursor (denoted resol) was slightly modified from the basic preparation described in the litterature26. The polymerization took place in basic conditions starting with phenol and formaldehyde. Typical phenolic resol preparation procedure is the following: 6.50 mmol phenol (Sigma Aldrich 99 %) was melted at 42 8C and then 0.65 mmol NaOH 20 wt.% (Sigma Aldrich ACS Reagent 97 %, pellets) was added slowly over 10 min under stirring. 13 mmol formaldehyde (Sigma Aldrich, 37 wt.% in H2O, contains 10–15 % methanol as stabilizer) was added drop-wise, and the reaction mixture was stirred at 72 8C for 30 min. After cooling the mixture to room temperature, the pH value of the reaction mixture was adjusted to 8.0 using a 0.6 mol L 1 HCl (37 % AnalaR NORMAPUR ) aqueous solution. Water was then evaporated under vacuum below 50 8C and the final product was re-dissolved in 10 mL absolute ethanol. In parallel, 2.1 mmol Cu(NO3)2.3H2O was dissolved in 15 mL absolute ethanol, containing 1.0 g of Pluronic F-127. To obtain complete dissolution, the mixture was stirred at 1000 rpm for 30 min at 21 8C. Then, the phenolic resol solution was slowly dropped into the Pluronic-Copper nitrate solution under stirring (600 rpm) which was maintained for 30 min. Then, the mixture was disposed in four Petri dishes and dried under fume hood at 21 8C overnight. Thermo-polymerization was conducted at 100 8C for 24 h and carbonization was performed at 350 or 500 8C for 3 h with a heating rate of 5 8C min 1 under Argon atmosphere with a flow rate of 7 L min 1. The final products were denoted as Cu/FDU-15-T, where T represents the carbonization temperature as Cu/FDU-15-350 and Cu/FDU-15-500. In addition, FDU-15-T samples were prepared by using the same procedure but without adding the Cu salt precursor.

sections.heading: N2 Physisorption
sections.text: Measurements of N2 sorption isotherms at 77 K were conducted by using a Micromeritics Tristar 3000 device. The prepared catalysts were previously degassed at 90 8C for 1 h and then at 350 8C for 4 h, up to a residual pressure smaller than 0.5 Pa. The specific surface area and pore size distribution (PSD) were determined by the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) method[35] and Barret-JoynerHalenda (BJH) analysis,[36] respectively, using the adsorption branch. Microporous volume was calculated by difference between the total pore volume (determined at P/P8= 0.95) and the mesopore volume determined by BJH method.

sections.heading: Thermo-Gravimetric (TG) Analysis
sections.text:
TG analyses were achieved by TA Instruments SDT Q600 apparatus equipped with TA Universal analysis software. Roughly, 15 mg of the sample was placed in alumina crucible then thermally heated under air flow of 100 mL min 1 from 25 to 800 8C with a heating rate of 5 C min 1. Just after, the burned powders were analyzed by XRD, confirming the carbon-free CuO formation.
Powder X-ray Diffraction

sections.heading: Cross-Section Transmission Electron Microscopy (CS-TEM) Coupled by Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy Analysis
sections.text: Sample preparation for CS-TEM: sample is embedded in a polymeric resin (Epon) at 60 8C for 48 h before cutting by using diamond knifes with ultra-microtome (Leica UCR RT) in the section thickness between 50 and 70 nm. CS-TEM lattice images were obtained by JEOL JEM-2100VRP electron microscope working at 200 kV accelerating voltage with LaB6 emitter. The point and linear resolution were 0.19 nm and 0.14 nm, respectively. The pointdissolved EDX analysis was performed at 200 kV equipped with a LaB6 filament and a CCD camera (Gatan Ultrascan 2Kx2K) attached to the microscope.

sections.heading: Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM)
sections.text: STEM analyses were carried out by using a JEOL 2100F microscope working at 200 kV, equipped with a Cs probe corrector and a GATAN Tridiem imaging filter. For the analyses, the samples were dispersed in ethanol (99.9 %) and then a drop of solution was deposited onto a TEM grid covered by a holey carbon membrane. The emission current was kept constant at 160 mA. The inner and outer angles for the HAADF detector were 52 and 140 mrad, respectively.

sections.heading: Electron Tomography (3D-TEM)
sections.text:
For obtaining the 3D reconstructions, a tilt series in the angular interval of 748 was acquired for each composite. The angular increment was set to 28. The tilt series were aligned using the cross-correlation method implemented in the IMOD software. The reconstructions were performed using the SIRT algorithm with 30 iterations, implemented in the Tomo3D software.

sections.heading: CO2 Electrolysis
sections.text: Catalytic ink for cyclic voltammetry is composed of a mixture of 90 vol.% isopropyl alcohol (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.5 %) and 10 vol.% of Nafion suspension (5 wt.% Sigma-Aldrich) + a mass of catalyst corresponding to 4 mg of Cu per mL ink. This means that for 1 mL of ink, 29.7 mg of Cu FDU15-350 and 22.9 mg of Cu FDU15-500 are weighted. Then, 5 mL of ink are drop casted onto the glassy carbon electrode (5 mm diameter). This leads to precisely 103 mg of Cu per cm2 electrode. For electrolysis experiments, electrochemical measurements were conducted using a bi-potentiostat (AUTOLABPGSTAT 302N) in a H-type cell in the three-electrode configuration. The counter and pseudo-reference electrode are Pt/IrO2 grid and Ag jAgCl, respectively. All the potentials applied were converted to reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) reference scale. The electrode loading (in mg of catalyst per cm2 of electrode) uses the same catalytic ink, but the volume of ink deposited onto the electrode is adapted to the final loading desired. An electrode loading of 1.59, 3.18, 4.77 and 6.36 mg of catalyst cm 2 was deposited onto the wet proofed Toray carbon paper (6.3 cm2 geometric area) and the solvent was evaporated at room temperature overnight. Corresponding Cu loadings are 216, 432, 649 and 865 mg of Cu per cm2 electrode for Cu/FDU-15-350 and 280, 560, 840 and 1119 mg of Cu per cm2 electrode for Cu/FDU-15-500. Electrolysis measurements were conducted in a homemade divided H-type electrochemical cell separated by an ion exchange Nafion -117 membrane. The cell was designed to have a large electrolyte volume of 100 cm3 in each compartment, along with a gas headspace of approximately 65 cm3 above the electrolyte. Cyclic voltammograms were recorded from 1.40 to 1.20 V vs. RHE at a scan rate of 50 mV s 1. Prior to electrolysis, 0.5 mol L 1 NaHCO3 aqueous solution was de-aerated by N2 for 20 min, and then saturated by CO2 gas for another 20 min with the pH value of 8.52 and 7.14, respectively. Electrolyses were conducted in the CO2-saturated electrolyte (2 bars) at various cathodic potentials ranging from 0.47, to 0.82 V vs. RHE with an electrode loading of 3.18 mg cm 2 at room temperature. Corresponding chronoamperograms along with electric charge and electrolysis duration can be found in supporting information (Figure S11 and table S11 and table S4).

sections.heading: Gas-Phase Analysis
sections.text: Gas products were quantified with online gas chromatography (Agilent Technologies, 490 m-GC). The residual reactant and/or product gases from the outlet of the cathodic compartment were vented directly into the gas-sampling loop of the GC, equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) that possesses three channels calibrated at different temperatures. The first one was equipped with a packed M5 A HBF column at 80 8C for H2 detection. The second channel contained a packed PPQH column at 60 8C for hydrocarbon (CxHy) detection, and the third one was equipped with a packed COX HBF column at 120 8C for CO2 and CO detection. Argon (Airgas, 99.999 %) and helium (Airgas, 99.999 %) were used as the carrier gases to quantify hydrogen and CO concentrations, respectively.

sections.heading: Liquid-Phase Analysis
sections.text: Liquid phase samples were analyzed by high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) which was equipped with Aminex HPX87H Ion Exclusion Column, Dionex Ultimate 3000 Pump, ASI-100 Automated Sample Injector and UV-detector. A 3.0 mM sulfuric acid solution was used as the mobile phase at 25 8C with a flow rate of 0.60 mL min 1.
